newsitem.title: UK: Central bank official urges anti-fraud vigilance.
newsitem.headline: Central bank official urges anti-fraud vigilance.

text.p: Financial crime will flourish if regulators, bankers and financial centres fail to keep their guard up, a senior Bank of England official said on Thursday.

Michael Foot, the central bank's executive director for supervision and surveillance, said in a speech prepared for a crime prevention conference in the Cayman Islands that developments in the financial markets over the next 10 years would be at least as great as they have been over the last 10.
Foot said that in some cases, such as those experienced in the Internet, "challenge may appear in novel form".
"It would be a complacent banker or regulator who did not start from the assumption that the next 10 years may see at least as much change as have the last 10," he said.

"Complacency would also be the charge for any regulator, banker or centre which did not recognise that, in such a climate, constant vigilance is necessary if financial crime in any of its forms is not to flourish," he said.

Foot highlighted the importance of the recent banking accord between the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, which is made up of supervisors from 10 countries, and the Offshore Group, comprising Cayman and 18 centres with similar interests.

"Only time will tell how this initiative develops. But I do predict that host countries which do not commit wholeheartedly to putting into effect the spirit of the accord which has been worked out so painstakingly may quickly find themselves regarded by others as "beyond the pale'," he said.

The Supervision of Cross-Border Banking accord was endorsed by 140 banking supervisory authorities at an international conference in Stockholm in June 1996. It sets out the appropriate relationships and flows of information between home and host country supervisors.
Countries agreed to look at their own legislation and procedures over the next two years to ensure they were consistent with the accord and alter them if they were not.
Foot also detailed the benefits of a steady rise in international standards and the effects of international cooperation in the fight against money-laundering.
It was important money-laundering should not be seen as merely a problem for off-shore centres such as the Caymans.

"London and Cayman share a common problem brought about in part by their very success as financial centres. The size and freedom of their markets make them an attractive target for the launderer," Foot said.

This meant a need for cooperation and strong safeguards, while still respecting the "legitimate interests of the sevice providers and their customers". But it also entailed a financial cost, as with other aspects of modern regulation, Foot said.

"I have to acknowledge that the maintenance of adequate anti-money-laundering standards is undoubtedly going to involve additional expenditure by the authorities and perhaps by the banks themselves," he added.

Changes in financial markets would also mean a need for "continuing enhancement of the skill and resource base for supervisors worldwide" as well as "further tightening of legislation to fill gaps and plug loopholes".
Moves by the Cayman Islands to strengthen their own regulatory structure were in keeping with this trend.
